sections.html:
Washington County sits in eastern Nebraska just north of Douglas County and the Omaha area, with Blair as the county seat. About 20,865 people live in the county. Most of the land is farmland, with Blair and Fort Calhoun as the cities and Arlington, Herman, Kennard and Washington as villages.

A homeowner here may live in a town, in a village or on a rural parcel, and that choice decides which municipal rules apply on top of the county's. Low ground near the Missouri River carries flood risk, as the 2011 river floods near the Blair bridge showed.

sections.h2: Selling in Blair or a village
sections.html:
Blair is the county seat, and the villages of Arlington, Herman, Kennard and Washington sit around it, with Fort Calhoun as the other city. A buyer will want to know which of these, or which rural parcel, the house belongs to, because that decides which municipal rules and levies apply. Cash buyers do not need a lender's appraisal, so a farmhouse, an inherited house or a house with deferred repairs can still sell.

Many Blair buyers work in the Omaha and Council Bluffs area, so commuting distance is a talking point. If the house sits on low ground near the Missouri River, tell the buyer before the inspection, since the 2011 flooding near the Blair bridge is part of the county's recent history and the lender may ask about flood insurance.

Before you list, collect the last tax statement, your protest paperwork if you filed one, and any homestead exemption confirmation. Then call the Treasurer at (402) 426-6888 for the balance and the Clerk at (402) 426-6822 if a protest is pending.

Four county offices touch a property owner, each with its own task.

sections.h2: How Nebraska values a home here
sections.html:
The assessment date is January 1. Houses, rural homes, buildings, commercial and industrial property, recreational property and mobile homes are held to 100 percent of market value, while agricultural land is held to 75 percent and priced from soil maps and land use such as dry, irrigated or grassland.

To get the bill, the county multiplies taxable value by the consolidated rate for your district, quoted per $100. A parcel in a town pays county, municipal and school levies together. That is why two houses of equal value can receive unequal bills when they lie in separate districts.

A changed value brings a notice from the assessor by June 1, addressed to the owner of record on May 20. Separately, qualifying owners may shield part or all of a home's value through the homestead exemption. File that application with the assessor between February 1 and June 30.

Your protest goes on Form 422, filed with the County Clerk by June 30. Begin with a call to the Assessor's staff, since an explanation may make the protest unnecessary.

  1. Ask the Assessor's office how your value was reached.
  2. File Form 422 with the Clerk by June 30. State the value you want, your reasons and the legal description, because a protest with no reasons can be dismissed.
  3. Request an Assessor review if you want one. A referee who is a registered appraiser may meet you before the Board of Equalization hearing.
  4. Go to the hearing. The Clerk sets the time and place and sends the Board's decision within seven days of the final action.
  5. Still unhappy? The Tax Equalization and Review Commission takes appeals filed within 30 days after the Board adjourns. For the June 1 to July 25 session, adjournment is deemed July 25.

Protests cover valuation, never the tax rate. For a house, the best evidence is comparable sales or a recent appraisal. Personal property protests are due earlier, by May 1.

Real and personal property taxes fall due December 31. After that, May 1 is the delinquency date for the first half and September 1 for the second. Interest on delinquent taxes owed to political subdivisions is 14 percent a year under Nebraska law. Douglas County uses different dates, so owners who moved up from Omaha need new reminders.

Send checks to the Washington County Treasurer, P.O. Box 348, Blair, NE 68008, or use the county's online payment vendor. Personal property tax becomes a first lien on everything of that kind you own as of the due date, and the property can be seized to satisfy it.

Nebraska Revised Statute 77-1801 links the county tax sale of delinquent real property to the first Monday of March. Statute 77-1802 has the county treasurer prepare a list of delinquent parcels four to six weeks ahead of that Monday. Back taxes on your house? Request a payoff figure from the Treasurer right away. More choices stay open, whether you pay, sell or negotiate, the earlier you know the total.

At closing, the title company normally pays any tax owed out of your proceeds and divides the current year's bill between the parties. A house with delinquent taxes can still close, since the payoff generally comes out of the price.

  • Phone the Treasurer at (402) 426-6888 for a balance before signing anything.
  • Request the title company's settlement statement ahead of signing day.
  • Make sure no earlier year remains open.

Rural parcels need an extra check. Because a country property may sit in a different school or levy district than a house in town, confirm the district on your bill before you quote taxes to a buyer.

Washington County sales are recorded by the Register of Deeds, which charges $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page, plus $1.50 a page for certified copies. Send a Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, with the deed.

The grantor owes Nebraska's documentary stamp tax of $3.32 on each $1,000 of value (fractions count) for deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later. Plan for the state figure when you budget for closing.

faqs.q: When is the Washington County, Nebraska property tax protest deadline?
faqs.a: File with the County Clerk on or before June 30 for real property, or by May 1 for personal property. Use Form 422, name the value you want and say why.

faqs.q: When do Washington County taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: After the December 31 due date, the first half goes delinquent after May 1 and the second after September 1. Nebraska law sets interest at 14 percent a year, and mail payments go to P.O. Box 348 in Blair or can be made online.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house in Washington County if I owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company normally pays back taxes from the proceeds at closing and confirms the payoff. Phone the Treasurer at (402) 426-6888 for a balance first.

faqs.q: Who do I call to dispute my Washington County property value?
faqs.a: Talk to the County Assessor's office first. If the issue remains, file Form 422 with the County Clerk, 1555 Colfax Street in Blair, phone (402) 426-6822.

faqs.q: How is farmland valued compared with a house?
faqs.a: A house is valued at 100 percent of market. Farmland is held to 75 percent and priced from soil maps and use.
